blocks.text: How does an operating system decide which process to run next? The answer lies in understanding scheduling criteria like throughput, turnaround time, waiting time, and response time.

blocks.markdown: In operating systems, CPU scheduling is crucial for efficient process management. The scheduler decides which process runs at any given time, aiming to optimize certain criteria. Let's explore these criteria and understand how they impact scheduling decisions.

blocks.title: Throughput
blocks.text: Throughput is the number of processes that complete their execution per time unit. It is a measure of work done by the system.

blocks.title: Turnaround Time
blocks.text: Turnaround time is the total time taken from the submission of a process to its completion. It includes both waiting and execution time.

blocks.title: Waiting Time
blocks.text: Waiting time is the total time a process spends waiting in the ready queue before it gets CPU time.

blocks.title: Response Time
blocks.text: Response time is the time from submission of a request until the first response is produced, not the completion of the process.

blocks.markdown: These criteria often conflict. For instance, optimizing for throughput might increase waiting time, as more processes are completed, but individual processes may wait longer.

blocks.title: Calculating Turnaround Time
blocks.prompt: Consider three processes with the following burst times: P1 = 10ms, P2 = 5ms, and P3 = 8ms. They arrive in the order P1, P2, P3. Calculate the turnaround time for each process assuming a non-preemptive scheduling algorithm.

steps.text: Determine the completion time for each process.

blocks.answer: Turnaround times are 10ms, 15ms, and 23ms for P1, P2, and P3, respectively.

blocks.markdown: Now, let's distinguish between preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling. Preemptive scheduling allows a process to be interrupted and moved to the ready queue, whereas non-preemptive scheduling runs a process to completion once it starts.

blocks.title: Impact of Scheduling Type
blocks.prompt: Given the same processes as before, calculate the waiting time for each process using a preemptive scheduling algorithm like Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF).

steps.text: Determine the order of execution using SRTF.

blocks.answer: Waiting times are 13ms, 0ms, and 5ms for P1, P2, and P3, respectively.

blocks.title: Trade-offs in Scheduling
blocks.text: Optimizing one scheduling criterion often comes at the expense of another. For example, minimizing waiting time may reduce throughput.

points: Throughput, turnaround time, waiting time, and response time are key scheduling criteria.
Preemptive scheduling can improve response time but may increase overhead.
Optimizing one criterion can negatively impact others, requiring careful balance.
